newsitem.title: LATVIA: New Latvian government comes to power.
newsitem.headline: New Latvian government comes to power.

text.p: Latvian Prime Minister Andris Shkele won parliamentary support on Thursday for his new government, which aims to keep the small Baltic state on the path of economic reform and holds open the post of finance minister which caused a political crisis in January.
Parliament backed the government by 70 votes in favour and 17 against in the 100-seat parliament.
The government is Shkele's second since he came to power at the end of 1995 and is formed from eight parties in Latvia's splintered parliament.
His previous government was strongly reformist, aiming to boost the economic reforms launched after Latvia regained its independence from the former Soviet Union in 1991.
"It will not be easy but this cabinet will work better," Shkele told journalists after the vote.
Asked whether economic reforms would go faster now, Shkele said: "We have all the dates in our declaration. If we manage (to fulfill it) no one will have to be ashamed."
Shkele first came to power with the specific aim of solving Latvia's economic problems in the wake of a serious banking crisis in mid-1995.
He has helped to speed privatisation and passed a balanced budget for 1997.
Shkele was forced to form a second government after a surprise resignation in January.
The resignation was caused after a row with President Guntis Ulmanis over the nomination of a finance minister who had been investigated by the prosecutor's office.
Ulmanis called on parliament to reject the proposed minister, Vassily Melnik, infuriating Shkele.
Ulmanis and Shkele later settled their differences and the president called on Shkele to form a second government. Melnik resigned two days after he was appointed.
The finance post in Shkele's latest cabinet is still vacant and will be held temporarily by the prime minister.
He said that he would get cross-party support for any proposed finance minister.
"The line up of this government is better than the previous one. Instead of 29 ministers we now have 18," Shkele added.
